title: Feelings about racism; black heroes of Cuban independence
summary: Machito answers about inferiority complexes by citing Maceo and Bandera, and gives his view of the Maine and US interest in Cuba.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: Macho, since you were one of the ones discriminated against, How did you feel? Tell me exactly what you felt when a country - when a country

Well, I have a different opinion about the the way - - I felt very bad because my grandfather was white and he was a gentleman and it was a legitimate - legitimate marriage, it was no flight-by-night; so I feel bad because my my grandfather was a gentleman and he treat my mother like a princess......
No, but you yourself and other Afro-Cubans, Were there any complexes because they were black and made to feel inferior because of a racist government that instilled this in the public mind?
Well, the most important thing is that the greatest warrior, the greatest guy in the Cuban independence, was black. Quintin Bandera, the whole family of Maceo, there was about five.......

The mother of Antonio Maceo, Jose Maceo, and two or three more Maceos, they died for the revolution. So when the ah - when the United States put the Main in the Habana harbor and blew up and I don't know if it was a accident or was a purpose to declare the war to Spain, because geographically or strategically United States need Cuba for the Panama, Canal de Panama, like Puerto Rico. They was looking for -'for protection. Geographically, Cuba and Puerto Rico was practically the backbone of the defense for the canal they were building.
Okay, I got the political picture now.
